questions.stem: \(1+2i\) is a root of the equation \(z^3-z^2+qz+5=0\). The value of \(q\) is:
questions.hint: Use the conjugate root, find the third root from the product of roots, then use the sum of pairwise products.

questions.stem:
\(P(z)=z^4-10z^3+117z^2-412z+1460\).
\(P(z)\) has zeroes \(2a+bi\) and \(3a+2bi\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are integers.

parts.stem: Find the values of \(a\) and \(b\) and hence find all the zeroes of \(P(z)\).
parts.hint: Use the sum of zeroes for a, then the product of zeroes for b.

steps.explain: Real coefficients, so the conjugates are zeroes too.
Sum of the zeroes \(=-\frac ba=10\). The imaginary parts cancel.
Product of the zeroes \(=\frac ea=1460\). Multiply conjugate pairs: \((p+qi)(p-qi)=p^2+q^2\).
Solve as a quadratic in \(b^2\).
\(b\) is an integer, so \(b^2=16\), \(b=\pm4\). The zeroes are \(2\pm4i\) and \(3\pm8i\).

keyPoints.note: Include the conjugates. Sum of zeroes gives a; product of zeroes gives a quadratic in b².

parts.stem: Factorise \(P(z)\) into its quadratic factors with real coefficients.
parts.hint: Each conjugate pair p ± qi gives z² − 2pz + (p² + q²).

For \(2\pm4i\): sum 4, product \(4+16=20\).
For \(3\pm8i\): sum 6, product \(9+64=73\).
So

keyPoints.note: Pair each zero with its conjugate: z² − (sum)z + (product).

parts.stem: Explain why \(z^4=(z-1)^4\) does not have four roots.
parts.hint: Expand: the z⁴ terms cancel.

steps.explain: Move everything to one side and expand.
The \(z^4\) terms cancel, leaving a polynomial of degree 3. A degree-3 polynomial has at most 3 roots.

options: Because the equation only has real roots.
Expanding, \(z^4-(z-1)^4\) is a cubic (the \(z^4\) terms cancel), so it has at most 3 roots.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: z⁴ − (z − 1)⁴ — what is its degree?

parts.hint: Let x = z/(z − 1) so x⁴ = 1; solve each case for z.

steps.explain: \(z=1\) is not a solution, so divide by \((z-1)^4\) and let \(x=\frac{z}{z-1}\).
\(x=1\): \(z=z-1\) — impossible. \(x=-1\): \(z=1-z\Rightarrow z=\frac12\).
The cubic has real coefficients, so the conjugate is also a root (it comes from \(x=-i\)).

keyPoints.note: Divide by (z − 1)⁴: (z/(z − 1))⁴ = 1, so z/(z − 1) is a fourth root of unity.

questions.hint: Use Vieta’s formulas. First note that the two non-real cube roots are conjugates, so \(\omega+\bar\omega=-1\) and \(\omega\bar\omega=1\).

steps.explain: The non-real cube root has argument \(2\pi/3\), hence \(\omega+\bar\omega=2\cos(2\pi/3)=-1\) and \(\omega\bar\omega=1\).
For a monic cubic, the sum of roots is \(-a\). The roots sum to \(1-\omega-\bar\omega=2\).
The sum of pairwise products is b, and the product of all three roots is \(-c\).

questions.stem: Let \(\omega = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{5} + i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}\). Which of the following polynomials has \(\omega, \omega^3, \omega^7\) and \(\omega^9\) as its zeros?
questions.hint: Use the conjugate pairs of roots. The product of \((z-\alpha)(z-\bar\alpha)\) is \(z^2 - 2\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)z + |\alpha|^2\).

steps.explain: Write the roots using de Moivre: \(\omega = e^{\frac{\pi}{5}i}\). Then \(\omega^3 = e^{\frac{3\pi}{5}i}\), \(\omega^7 = e^{\frac{7\pi}{5}i}\), \(\omega^9 = e^{\frac{9\pi}{5}i}\). Note \(\omega^7 = \bar{\omega}^3\) and \(\omega^9 = \bar\omega\).
Pair the roots into conjugates. \((z-\omega)(z-\bar\omega)=z^2-2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}z+1\) and \((z-\omega^3)(z-\bar\omega^3)=z^2-2\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{5}z+1\).

Expand. The \(z^3\) coefficient is \(-2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}-2\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{5}=-1\), since \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}+\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{5}=\dfrac12\). The \(z^2\) coefficient is \(2+4\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{5}=1\).
Check the constant term: \(1\times1=1\). Options A, B and C have the wrong signs on the z terms.

keyPoints.note: Each root and its conjugate give a quadratic factor.

questions.stem: Hence, by solving \(16x^4-16x^2+1=0\) using the substitution \(x=\cos\theta\), prove that \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{12}=\dfrac{1}{16}\).
questions.answer: With \(x=\cos\theta\), \(16x^4-16x^2+1=2(8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1)-1=2\cos4\theta-1\). So \(\cos4\theta=\dfrac12\). The four roots are \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12},\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{12},\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\), whose product is \(\dfrac{1}{16}\) (product of roots \(=\dfrac{e}{a}=\dfrac{1}{16}\)).
questions.hint: Use the identity from part (i) to rewrite \(16x^4-16x^2+1\) as \(2\cos4\theta-1\).

steps.explain: Use part (i): \(8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1=\cos4\theta\). So \(16x^4-16x^2+1=2(8x^4-8x^2+1)-1=2\cos4\theta-1\).
Set this to zero: \(2\cos4\theta-1=0\), so \(\cos4\theta=\dfrac12\). Then \(4\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\dfrac{7\pi}{3},\dfrac{11\pi}{3}\) in the first period.
Divide by 4 to get \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{7\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\). These are the four roots \(x_1,\dots,x_4\).
The polynomial \(16x^4-16x^2+1\) has product of roots \(\dfrac{e}{a}=\dfrac{1}{16}\) (for degree 4, the product is the constant term divided by the leading coefficient).
So \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{12}=\dfrac{1}{16}\). Proof complete.

questions.stem: Solve \(4z^3 - iz^2 - 4z + i = 0\) over the set of complex numbers.
questions.hint: Multiply by \(i\) to remove the complex coefficients. Then test simple values with the remainder theorem.

steps.explain: Multiply every term by \(i\): \(4iz^3+z^2-4iz-1=0\). Real coefficients are now easier to test.
Test \(z=-\dfrac{1}{4i}=\dfrac{i}{4}\): \(4i\left(\dfrac{i}{4}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{i}{4}\right)^2-4i\left(\dfrac{i}{4}\right)-1=0\). So \(z=\dfrac{i}{4}\) is the third root.
A cubic has three roots, so these are all of them. Check the product: \(1\times(-1)\times\dfrac{i}{4}=-\dfrac{i}{4}\), which matches \(-\dfrac{d}{a}\) for the cubic.

questions.stem: Consider the equation \(z^5=1\). Show that for \(z\ne1\): \(\dfrac{z^5-1}{z-1}=\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+1\right)\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}+1\right)\).
questions.answer: The roots of \(z^5-1=0\) are \(1\), \(\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)\), \(\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right)\). Pair each conjugate pair: \((z-\text{cis}\theta)(z-\text{cis}(-\theta))=z^2-2z\cos\theta+1\). Then \(z^5-1=(z-1)\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+1\right)\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}+1\right)\). ∎
questions.hint: Factorise \(z^5-1\) using ALL its roots from (i), then group the CONJUGATE roots in pairs (each pair gives a real quadratic).

steps.explain: Factor theorem with the five roots from (i).
Divide by \(z-1\) (\(z\ne1\)).
Multiply a conjugate pair: sum of roots \(\omega+\bar{\omega}=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) and product \(\omega\bar{\omega}=|\omega|^2=1\).
The same for the second pair (angle \(\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\)).
Combine.

keyPoints.note: Factorise the polynomial using all five roots and pair the conjugates.

questions.stem: Consider the polynomial \(\psi_n(x)=x^{4n+1}+(x+1)^{2n-1}\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Show that \(\psi_n(\omega)=0\) and that \(\psi_n\left(\omega^2\right)=0\).
questions.answer: Use \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\) and \(\omega^3=1\). Then \(\omega+1=-\omega^2\), so \(\psi_n(\omega)=\omega^{4n+1}+\left(-\omega^2\right)^{2n-1}=\omega^{4n+1}-\omega^{4n-2}=\omega^{4n-2}\left(\omega^3-1\right)=0\). For \(\omega^2\): \(\omega^2+1=-\omega\), so \(\psi_n\left(\omega^2\right)=\omega^{8n+2}+(-\omega)^{2n-1}=\omega^{8n+2}-\omega^{2n-1}=\omega^{2n-1}\left(\omega^{6n+3}-1\right)=\omega^{2n-1}\left(\left(\omega^3\right)^{2n+1}-1\right)=0\).
questions.hint: Use \(\omega+1=-\omega^2\) (from part (i)) and \(\omega^3=1\) to reduce the powers.

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\omega+1=-\omega^2\) and \(\omega^2+1=-\omega\).
For \(\omega\): \((\omega+1)^{2n-1}=(-\omega^2)^{2n-1}=-\omega^{4n-2}\) (odd power).
Since \(\omega^{6n+3}=\left(\omega^3\right)^{2n+1}=1\), this is 0. ✓

keyPoints.note: Use ω + 1 = −ω² and ω³ = 1.

questions.stem: Hence, show that \(x^2+x+1\) is a factor of \(\psi_n(x)=x^{4n+1}+(x+1)^{2n-1}\).
questions.answer: \(x^2+x+1=0\) has roots \(\omega\) and \(\omega^2\) (the non-real cube roots of unity). Both are zeros of \(\psi_n(x)\) (part ii), and \(\psi_n\) has real coefficients, so \((x-\omega)\left(x-\omega^2\right)=x^2+x+1\) divides \(\psi_n(x)\) with no remainder.
questions.hint: The roots of \(x^2+x+1=0\) are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^2\). If both are zeros of \(\psi_n\), then the quadratic is a factor.

steps.explain: From part (ii) both \(\omega\) and \(\omega^2\) are zeros of \(\psi_n(x)\).
So \((x-\omega)\) and \((x-\omega^2)\) are factors, and \((x-\omega)(x-\omega^2)=x^2-(\omega+\omega^2)x+\omega^3=x^2+x+1\) is a factor of \(\psi_n(x)\). ✓

keyPoints.note: Both roots of x² + x + 1 are zeros of the polynomial.

questions.stem: The polynomial \(P(x)=x^{3}-5x^{2}+ax+b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real, has one root at \(x=3-2\sqrt{2}\,i\). Find the values of \(a\) and \(b\).
questions.hint: The coefficients are REAL, so complex roots come in CONJUGATE pairs. Use the sum of the roots to find the third root, then the sum of products in pairs (for \(a\)) and the product of all roots (for \(b\)).

steps.explain: Real coefficients: the conjugate \(3+2\sqrt{2}\,i\) is also a root. Let the third root be \(r\).
Sum of roots \(=-\dfrac{-5}{1}=5\). The two complex roots add to 6.
Product of all roots \(=-b\) (for a cubic with leading coefficient 1). First \((3-2\sqrt{2}i)(3+2\sqrt{2}i)=9+8=17\).
Sum of the products of the roots in pairs \(=a\). Pairs: \(17\) (the two complex roots) and \(r\times\) each complex root, which add to \(r\times6\).
So \(a=11\) and \(b=17\). Check: \(P(-1)=-1-5-11+17=0\) ✓. Why not the others: B and C have a sign error (\(b=-17\) from product \(=b\); \(a=-11\) from sign of the pair sum); D swaps \(a\) and \(b\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Conjugate root theorem; sum, pairs and product of roots.

questions.stem: The complex number \(1+i\) is a zero of the polynomial \(P(z)=z^{4}-2z^{3}+z^{2}+2z-2\). Find the remaining zeros of the polynomial.
questions.hint: \(P\) has REAL coefficients, so complex zeros come in CONJUGATE pairs: \(1-i\) is also a zero. Multiply the pair of factors to get a quadratic, divide it out, and solve what is left.

steps.explain: Real coefficients \(\Rightarrow\) conjugate root theorem: \(1+i\) a zero \(\Rightarrow\) \(1-i\) a zero.
Quadratic factor from the pair: sum of roots \(=2\), product \(=(1+i)(1-i)=1+1=2\), so \(z^{2}-2z+2\).
Solve \(z^{2}-1=0\): difference of two squares.

Check \(P(1)=1-2+1+2-2=0\) ✓ and \(P(-1)=1+2+1-2-2=0\) ✓. Why not the others: B treats \(-1\pm i\) as zeros (wrong quadratic factor); C and D give zeros (2) that do not satisfy \(P(2)=16-16+4+4-2=6\ne0\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the remaining zeros of the polynomial.
keyPoints.note: Conjugate \(1-i\); divide by \(z^{2}-2z+2\).

parts.stem: Hence or otherwise show that \(w^7+64w=0\).
parts.hint: Use de Moivre's theorem on w = 2 cis(5π/6), then reduce the argument.

steps.explain: Use the result of part (i) and de Moivre's theorem \((r\operatorname{cis}\theta)^n=r^n\operatorname{cis}n\theta\).
Bring the argument into \((-\pi,\pi]\) by subtracting a multiple of \(2\pi\).
Now add \(64w\).
A shorter route: factor out \(w\) and use \(w^6\).

parts.answer: Using \(w=2\operatorname{cis}\frac{5\pi}{6}\) and de Moivre's theorem: \(w^7=2^7\operatorname{cis}\frac{35\pi}{6}=128\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{35\pi}{6}-6\pi\right)=128\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=128\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac12i\right)=64\sqrt3-64i\). Also \(64w=-64\sqrt3+64i\). Adding, \(w^7+64w=0\). (Alternatively \(w^6=64\operatorname{cis}5\pi=-64\), so \(w^7+64w=w(w^6+64)=0\).)

keyPoints.note: Apply de Moivre to 2 cis(5π/6); 35π/6 − 6π = −π/6.

questions.stem:
The argument of a complex number \(z\) is \(\frac{\pi}{7}\).
What is \(\operatorname{Arg}\left(z^{10}\right)\) equal to?
questions.hint: Multiply the argument by 10, then bring it into (−π, π] by subtracting 2π.

steps.explain: Write \(z\) in modulus–argument form.
By de Moivre's theorem, raising to the 10th power multiplies the argument by 10.
\(\operatorname{Arg}\) (capital A) means the principal argument, which must lie in \((-\pi,\pi]\). \(\frac{10\pi}{7}\gt\pi\), so subtract \(2\pi\).
So \(\operatorname{Arg}(z^{10})=\frac{-4\pi}{7}\), option D. (\(\frac{3\pi}{7}\) comes from subtracting only \(\pi\).)

keyPoints.note: Capital-A Arg is the principal argument: it must be in (−π, π].

steps.explain: Let \(x=\tan\theta\) and use (iii) with \(\tan4\theta=1\).

parts.answer: Let \(x=\tan\theta\) where \(\tan4\theta=1\). By (iii), \(\frac{4x-4x^3}{1-6x^2+x^4}=1\), so \(1-6x^2+x^4=4x-4x^3\), i.e. \(x^4+4x^3-6x^2-4x+1=0\). Choose the right root for \(x=\tan\frac\pi{16}\). Since \(0 \lt \frac\pi{16} \lt \frac\pi4\), we have \(0 \lt x \lt 1\), so \(\frac1x \gt 1 \gt x\) and \(u=x-\frac1x \lt 0\). Of the two roots, \(-2+2\sqrt2\approx0.83\) is positive, so
Numerical check: \(\tan\frac\pi{16}\approx0.1989\) and \(\cot\frac\pi{16}\approx5.0273\); the difference is \(\approx-4.828=-2-2\sqrt2\) ✓.

parts.answer: Divide the quartic by \(x^2\ (\neq0)\): \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}+4\left(x-\frac1x\right)-6=0\). Since \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=u^2+2\), this is \(u^2+4u-4=0\), so \(u=-2\pm2\sqrt2\). For \(x=\tan\frac\pi{16}\), \(0 \lt x \lt 1\) so \(u=x-\frac1x \lt 0\); the only negative root is \(-2-2\sqrt2\). Hence \(\tan\frac\pi{16}-\cot\frac\pi{16}=-2-2\sqrt2\).

questions.stem: Given \(z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), prove that \(z^{n}+\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}=2\cos n\theta\). Which proof is correct?
options: By De Moivre's theorem \(z^{n}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta\), and \(\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}=z^{-n}=\cos(-n\theta)+i\sin(-n\theta)=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta\). Adding, \(z^{n}+\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}=2\cos n\theta\).

\(z^{n}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta\) and \(\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}=-\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta\). Adding gives 0.

steps.explain: De Moivre's theorem: \((\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^{n}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta\).
\(\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}=z^{-n}\), and De Moivre's theorem also holds for \(-n\).
Cosine is even (\(\cos(-x)=\cos x\)) and sine is odd (\(\sin(-x)=-\sin x\)).
Add: the imaginary parts cancel.
Why not the others: B forgets the sign change of the sine; C wrongly applies the power to each part; D treats \(\dfrac{1}{z^{n}}\) as \(-z^{n}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Show that, when \(z\ne0\), \(1+2z+3z^{2}+\cdots+nz^{n-1}=\dfrac{z^{-1}-(n+1)z^{n-1}+nz^{n}}{z^{-1}-2+z}\). Which working is correct?
options: From (i): \(\dfrac{1-(n+1)z^{n}+nz^{n+1}}{(1-z)^{2}}\). Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(z\): numerator \(\to z^{-1}-(n+1)z^{n-1}+nz^{n}\); denominator \(\dfrac{(1-z)^{2}}{z}=\dfrac{1-2z+z^{2}}{z}=z^{-1}-2+z\).
From (i): divide only the numerator by \(z\), giving \(z^{-1}-(n+1)z^{n-1}+nz^{n}\), and leave the denominator \((1-z)^{2}\) unchanged.
From (i): multiply the numerator and the denominator by \(z\): numerator \(\to z-(n+1)z^{n+1}+nz^{n+2}\); denominator \(\to z(1-z)^{2}=z-2z^{2}+z^{3}\).
From (i): divide by \(z^{2}\): numerator \(\to z^{-2}-(n+1)z^{n-2}+nz^{n-1}\); denominator \(\to z^{-2}-2z^{-1}+1\).
questions.hint: Take the result of (i) and divide the TOP and the BOTTOM of the fraction by \(z\) (allowed because \(z\ne0\); this multiplies the fraction by \(\dfrac{1}{1}=1\)).

steps.explain: Start with the result of part (i), for \(z\ne1\).
Divide the numerator by \(z\) term by term: \(\dfrac{1}{z}=z^{-1}\), \(\dfrac{z^{n}}{z}=z^{n-1}\), \(\dfrac{z^{n+1}}{z}=z^{n}\).
Divide the denominator by \(z\): expand \((1-z)^{2}=1-2z+z^{2}\) first.
Put the two together (we divided top and bottom by the same non-zero \(z\), so the value is unchanged).
Why not the others: B divides only the top (changing the value); C multiplies instead of dividing; D divides by \(z^{2}\) (wrong powers).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Divide numerator and denominator of the part (i) result by z.

questions.stem: Hence, by writing \(z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) and using De Moivre’s Theorem, show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\cos(k-1)\theta=\dfrac{(n+1)\cos(n-1)\theta-n\cos n\theta-\cos\theta}{2(1-\cos\theta)}\). Which working is correct?
options: Put \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta\) in (iii): LHS \(=\sum k\,\text{cis}(k-1)\theta\); RHS \(=\dfrac{\text{cis}(-\theta)-(n+1)\text{cis}(n-1)\theta+n\,\text{cis}\,n\theta}{\text{cis}(-\theta)-2+\text{cis}\,\theta}\) with denominator \(2\cos\theta-2\). Equate REAL parts: \(\sum k\cos(k-1)\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta-(n+1)\cos(n-1)\theta+n\cos n\theta}{2\cos\theta-2}=\dfrac{(n+1)\cos(n-1)\theta-n\cos n\theta-\cos\theta}{2(1-\cos\theta)}\).
Put \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta\) in (iii) and equate IMAGINARY parts: \(\sum k\sin(k-1)\theta=\dfrac{-\sin\theta-(n+1)\sin(n-1)\theta+n\sin n\theta}{2\cos\theta-2}\).

Put \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta\) in (iii) and equate real parts, but write the denominator as \(2\cos\theta+2\): \(\sum k\cos(k-1)\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta-(n+1)\cos(n-1)\theta+n\cos n\theta}{2(1+\cos\theta)}\).

Put \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta\) in (iii) and divide the real part of the numerator by the real part of the denominator separately: \(\sum k\cos(k-1)\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta-(n+1)\cos(n-1)\theta+n\cos n\theta}{\cos\theta-2}\).
questions.hint: De Moivre: \(z^{m}=\cos m\theta+i\sin m\theta\). Put \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta\) in part (iii). The denominator \(z^{-1}-2+z\) is REAL (\(2\cos\theta-2\)), so equating real parts of both sides is easy: real part of the left side is \(\sum k\cos(k-1)\theta\).

steps.explain: Substitute \(z=\text{cis}\,\theta=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) into (iii). By De Moivre's theorem \(z^{m}=\text{cis}\,m\theta\), so the left side is \(1+2\text{cis}\,\theta+3\text{cis}\,2\theta+\cdots+n\,\text{cis}(n-1)\theta\).
Simplify the denominator: \(\text{cis}(-\theta)+\text{cis}\,\theta=2\cos\theta\) (the imaginary parts cancel), so it is the REAL number \(2\cos\theta-2\).
Since the denominator is real, take the real part of each side: the real part of \(\text{cis}\,m\theta\) is \(\cos m\theta\).
Use \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\) and multiply top and bottom by \(-1\) to turn \(2\cos\theta-2\) into \(2(1-\cos\theta)\).
Why not the others: B takes the imaginary parts (gives a \(\sin\) series); C has the wrong sign in the denominator; D divides real parts separately (not allowed).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Put z = cis theta, note the denominator is real, then take real parts.

questions.stem: By solving \(\tan5\theta=0\), deduce that \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{5}\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{5}\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=5\). Which argument is correct?
options: \(\tan5\theta=0\Rightarrow5\theta=0,\pi,2\pi,3\pi,4\pi\), so \(\theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{5},\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{3\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\). Also \(5t-10t^{3}+t^{5}=t(t^{4}-10t^{2}+5)=0\). The four non-zero roots of \(t^{4}-10t^{2}+5\) are \(\tan\dfrac{k\pi}{5}\) for \(k=1,2,3,4\). Product of roots \(=\dfrac{5}{1}=5\).
\(\tan5\theta=0\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{5},\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{3\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\). The roots of \(t^{4}-10t^{2}+5\) have product \(-\dfrac{5}{1}=-5\), so the product is \(-5\).
\(\tan5\theta=0\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{5},\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{3\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\). The roots of \(t^{4}-10t^{2}+5\) add to \(10\), so the product is \(10\).
\(\tan5\theta=0\Rightarrow\theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{5},\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{3\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\). All five roots of \(t(t^{4}-10t^{2}+5)\) multiply to 5, since the constant is 5.
questions.hint: Solve \(\tan5\theta=0\) in TWO ways: (1) by angles (\(5\theta\) is a multiple of \(\pi\)); (2) from the part (ii) numerator (\(5t-10t^{3}+t^{5}=0\)). Match the roots, then use the PRODUCT OF ROOTS formula for the quartic.

steps.explain: Angle method: \(\tan5\theta=0\) when \(5\theta\) is a multiple of \(\pi\). For \(0\le\theta<\pi\) that gives five values.
Algebra method: \(\tan5\theta=0\) when the numerator of part (ii) is 0.

For a quartic \(t^{4}+bt^{3}+ct^{2}+dt+e=0\) the product of the four roots is \(+e\) (even degree: sign \((-1)^{4}=+1\)). Here \(e=5\).
Why not the others: B uses the sign for an ODD-degree polynomial; C uses the sum of roots; D includes the root \(t=0\) (the product would then be 0).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Roots of the quartic = tan(kπ/5); product of roots = constant term.

questions.stem: Consider the equation \(z^5=(z+1)^5\) where \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). Solve \(z^5=(z+1)^5\), giving your answer in the form \(a+bi\cot\theta\) where \(a,b,\theta\in\mathbb{R}\).
questions.hint: Divide both sides by \(z^5\) (note \(z=0\) is not a root) to get \(\left(\dfrac{z+1}{z}\right)^5=1\), so \(\dfrac{z+1}{z}\) is a fifth root of unity. Then solve for \(z\) and use a half-angle identity.

steps.explain: Divide by \(z^5\).
So \(\dfrac{z+1}{z}=1+\dfrac{1}{z}=\omega\), a fifth root of unity, but \(\omega\ne1\) (else \(\dfrac{1}{z}=0\) is impossible).
Solve for \(z\).
Write \(\omega-1\) with half angles: \(\omega-1=\cos\theta-1+i\sin\theta=-2\sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}+2i\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), where \(\theta=\dfrac{2k\pi}{5}\).
Take the reciprocal: \(\dfrac{1}{\cos\phi+i\sin\phi}=\cos\phi-i\sin\phi\) with \(\phi=\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac{k\pi}{5}\).
Simplify: \(\dfrac{1}{i}=-i\).
All roots have real part \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\) (on a vertical line).

keyPoints.note: Divide by the fifth power of z; the ratio is a fifth root of unity.

questions.stem: If \(w\) is the root of \(z^{5}-1=0\) with the smallest positive argument, show that \(w^{2}+\dfrac{1}{w^{2}}+w+\dfrac{1}{w}=-1\). Which statements start the proof?
options: \(w=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\), the other roots are \(w^{2},w^{3},w^{4},1\), so \(1+w+w^{2}+w^{3}+w^{4}=0\); and \(\dfrac{1}{w}=w^{4}\), \(\dfrac{1}{w^{2}}=w^{3}\)
questions.hint: The sum of the roots of \(z^{5}-1=0\) is 0 (the \(z^{4}\) coefficient is 0). Also \(w^{5}=1\), so \(\dfrac{1}{w}=w^{4}\).

steps.explain: The root with the smallest positive argument is \(w=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). The other roots are its powers: \(w^{2},w^{3},w^{4}\) and \(w^{5}=1\).
The sum of the roots of \(z^{5}-1=0\) is 0 (the coefficient of \(z^{4}\) is 0).
Substitute into the left side: \(w^{2}+w^{3}+w+w^{4}\).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: Sum of the roots is zero; 1 over w equals w to the fourth since w to the fifth is 1.

questions.stem: Hence show that \(x=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) is a root of the equation \(4x^{2}+2x-1=0\). Which equation do you get after substituting \(w+\dfrac{1}{w}=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) and \(w^{2}+\dfrac{1}{w^{2}}=2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\)?
questions.hint: Use \(w+\dfrac{1}{w}=\operatorname{cis}\theta+\operatorname{cis}(-\theta)=2\cos\theta\), then the double angle formula \(\cos2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta-1\).

steps.explain: With \(w=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\), \(\dfrac{1}{w}=\operatorname{cis}\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)\). The sine parts cancel (sine is odd, cosine is even).
Similarly, \(w^{2}+\dfrac{1}{w^{2}}=2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\). Substitute both into part (ii).
Use the double angle formula \(\cos2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta-1\) with \(\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\): \(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=2\cos^{2}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}-1\).
Expand and rearrange.
So \(x=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) is a root of \(4x^{2}+2x-1=0\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Use the fact that a root plus its reciprocal is twice the cosine, then the double angle formula.

questions.stem: Hence find the exact value of \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). (Use that \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) is a root of \(4x^{2}+2x-1=0\).)
questions.hint: Solve the quadratic with the quadratic formula, then choose the root with the correct sign for the quadrant of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\).

steps.explain: Apply the quadratic formula to \(4x^{2}+2x-1=0\) (\(a=4,\ b=2,\ c=-1\)).
Simplify \(\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}\) and divide top and bottom by 2.
\(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}=72^\circ\) is in the FIRST quadrant, so its cosine is POSITIVE. Only \(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{4}\approx0.309\) is positive; \(\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{5}}{4}\approx-0.809\) is negative.
Check: \(\cos72^\circ\approx0.309\) \(\checkmark\).
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Quadratic formula, then choose the positive root (first quadrant).

questions.stem: Let \(\omega\) be a non-real fifth root of unity. Show that \(\omega^{4}+\omega^{3}+\omega^{2}+\omega+1=0\). Which argument is correct?
options: \(\omega^{5}=1\), so \(\omega^{4}=\dfrac{1}{\omega},\ \omega^{3}=\dfrac{1}{\omega^{2}}\), and the five terms add to \(\omega^{5}=1\ne0\).
Let \(\omega=\text{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). Then \(\omega+\omega^{4}=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) and the sum equals \(0\) for this one root only.
questions.hint: Start from \(\omega^{5}=1\), move everything to one side and FACTORISE \(\omega^{5}-1=(\omega-1)(\cdots)\). State why you may divide by \(\omega-1\).

steps.explain: A fifth root of unity satisfies \(\omega^{5}=1\). Rearrange to \(\omega^{5}-1=0\).
Factorise the difference of fifth powers: \(a^{5}-1=(a-1)(a^{4}+a^{3}+a^{2}+a+1)\).
A product is zero only if a factor is zero. \(\omega\) is NON-REAL, so \(\omega\ne1\) and \(\omega-1\ne0\).
Therefore the other factor is zero.
Why not the others: B never justifies dividing by \(\omega-1\); C is not a valid algebraic argument; D proves it for one specific root only (the question says ANY non-real fifth root).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Factorise omega to the fifth minus 1 and explain why omega minus 1 is not zero.

questions.stem: Let \(\omega\) be a non-real fifth root of unity, so \(\omega^{5}=1\) and \(\omega^{4}+\omega^{3}+\omega^{2}+\omega+1=0\). Prove that \(\omega-\omega^{4}\) is a root of the equation \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+5=0\). Which proof is correct?
options: \((\omega-\omega^{4})^{2}=\omega^{2}-\omega^{8}=\omega^{2}-\omega^{3}\). Then \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+5=(\omega^{2}-\omega^{3})^{2}+5(\omega^{2}-\omega^{3})+5=\omega^{4}-2\omega^{5}+\omega^{6}+5\omega^{2}-5\omega^{3}+5\), which does not simplify to 0.
Let \(\omega=\text{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). Substituting numerically gives a value near 0, so \(\omega-\omega^{4}\) is a root.
questions.hint: Square \(z=\omega-\omega^{4}\) first, reducing powers with \(\omega^{5}=1\) (so \(\omega^{6}=\omega,\ \omega^{8}=\omega^{3}\)). Then substitute into \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+5\) and use part (i).

steps.explain: Let \(z=\omega-\omega^{4}\) and square it, using \(\omega^{5}=1\) and \(\omega^{8}=\omega^{5}\cdot\omega^{3}=\omega^{3}\).
So \(z^{2}=\omega^{2}+\omega^{3}-2\). Now \(z^{4}=\left(z^{2}\right)^{2}\); expand with the pattern \((a+b-2)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+4+2ab-4a-4b\), \(a=\omega^{2},\ b=\omega^{3}\).
Reduce \(\omega^{6}=\omega\) and \(\omega^{5}=1\) (done above). Now form \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+5\).
Collect like terms: \(\omega^{2}:\ -4+5=1\); \(\omega^{3}:\ -4+5=1\); constants \(6-10+5=1\).
By part (i) this is 0, so \(z=\omega-\omega^{4}\) satisfies \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+5=0\).
Why not the others: B forgets the cross-term \(-2\omega^{5}\); C is numerical, not a proof, and only for one root; D wrongly uses \(\omega^{5}=0\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Square the expression, reduce powers with omega to the fifth equals 1, then use part (i).

questions.hint: The two square roots of any complex number are NEGATIVES of each other: \(w\) and \(-w\). On the Argand diagram, negating a point reflects it through the origin \(O\) (rotates it by \(180^{\circ}\)). Look for the pair that sits on opposite sides of \(O\) in a straight line through \(O\).

steps.explain: If \(w^{2}=z\) then \((-w)^{2}=z\) too, so the square roots are \(w\) and \(-w\): \(w_{2}=-w_{1}\).

Geometrically \(-w\) is the point obtained by going from \(w\) straight through \(O\) to the same distance on the other side (rotation by \(\pi\) about \(O\)). So the two roots and \(O\) are COLLINEAR with \(O\) in the middle (the midpoint).

Test each pair using the diagram: A (on the negative imaginary axis) and D (on the positive real axis) are not opposite; B (below the axis, right) and C (below the axis, left) have the SAME vertical side, so one cannot be minus the other; B (right, below) and E (right, above) are both on the right of \(O\).
C is to the LEFT of \(O\) and BELOW the real axis; E is to the RIGHT of \(O\) and ABOVE it — they are reflections of each other through \(O\), so \(E=-C\) (the line \(CE\) passes through \(O\)).

questions.stem: \(1\), \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) are the three cube roots of unity. Show that \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\) where \(\omega\) is a non-real root of unity.
questions.hint: \(\omega\) satisfies \(\omega^{3}=1\), so \(\omega^{3}-1=0\). Factorise the difference of cubes \(a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2})\). Since \(\omega\ne1\), the factor \(\omega-1\) is NOT zero, so the other factor must be.

steps.explain: Cube roots of unity satisfy \(z^{3}=1\), so \(\omega^{3}-1=0\).
Factorise (difference of cubes).
\(\omega\) is NON-REAL, so \(\omega\ne1\) and therefore \(\omega-1\ne0\). A product is zero only if a factor is zero, so the second factor must be zero.
Why not the others: B allows \(\omega=1\) (which is excluded) so cannot conclude; C expands \(\omega^{3}-1\) as \((\omega-1)^{3}\) (false); D gives no justification.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\omega^{3}-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^{2}+\omega+1)\), \(\omega\ne1\).

questions.stem: \(1\), \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) are the three cube roots of unity. Simplify each of the expressions \(\left(1+3\omega+\omega^{2}\right)^{2}\) and \(\left(1+\omega+3\omega^{2}\right)^{2}\).
questions.hint: Use \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\) to simplify INSIDE the bracket first: \(1+3\omega+\omega^{2}=(1+\omega+\omega^{2})+2\omega\). Then square and use \(\omega^{3}=1\).

steps.explain: Split off a zero: \(1+3\omega+\omega^{2}=(1+\omega+\omega^{2})+2\omega=0+2\omega\).
Square: \((2\omega)^{2}=4\omega^{2}\).
Similarly \(1+\omega+3\omega^{2}=(1+\omega+\omega^{2})+2\omega^{2}=2\omega^{2}\).
Square and use \(\omega^{3}=1\) to reduce \(\omega^{4}=\omega^{3}\cdot\omega=\omega\).
Why not the others: B swaps the two results; C and D make arithmetic slips (\(\left(2\omega\right)^{2}\ne2\omega^{2}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\) inside the bracket first; \(\omega^{3}=1\).

questions.stem: \(1\), \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) are the three cube roots of unity. Find \(\left(1+3\omega+\omega^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1+\omega+3\omega^{2}\right)^{2}\).
questions.hint: Use part (ii): the two squares are \(4\omega^{2}\) and \(4\omega\). Then factor \(4\) and use \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\).

steps.explain: From (ii) the two terms are \(4\omega^{2}\) and \(4\omega\).
Factor out 4.
From (i), \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\).
Why not the others: B drops the minus sign; C uses \(\omega+\omega^{2}=0\); D is the product from part (iv), not the sum.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(4\omega^{2}+4\omega=4(\omega+\omega^{2})=-4\).

questions.stem: \(1\), \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) are the three cube roots of unity. Find the product of \(\left(1+3\omega+\omega^{2}\right)^{2}\) and \(\left(1+\omega+3\omega^{2}\right)^{2}\).
questions.hint: Use part (ii) again: multiply \(4\omega^{2}\) and \(4\omega\), then use \(\omega^{3}=1\).

steps.explain: Multiply the two simplified results.
\(\omega\) is a cube root of unity: \(\omega^{3}=1\).

Why not the others: B has a wrong sign; C forgets that \(4\times4=16\); D forgets that \(\omega^{3}=1\) (it leaves \(\omega\) in the answer). Note: the sum is \(-4\) and the product \(16\), so these two squares are the roots of \(t^{2}+4t+16=0\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(4\omega^{2}\cdot4\omega=16\omega^{3}\), \(\omega^{3}=1\).

steps.explain: From the diagram: the angle \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) is drawn clockwise from the positive \(\mathrm{Re}\) axis to the ray, so \(\arg z^{2}=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), and \(|z^{2}|=4\).
Take the square root: \(\sqrt4=2\) and halve the argument: \(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\div2=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

The other square root is \(-z\): its argument is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\pi=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), which is in the 2nd quadrant. The question says \(z\) is in the FOURTH quadrant only, so we take \(\arg z=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (\(-60^{\circ}\): right and down).

questions.stem: Hence solve \(\left(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^{8}=-1\).
options: \(z=\pm i\cot\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{16}\), i.e. \(\pm i\cot\dfrac{\pi}{16},\ \pm i\cot\dfrac{3\pi}{16},\ \pm i\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{16},\ \pm i\cot\dfrac{7\pi}{16}\)
\(z=\pm i\tan\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{16}\), i.e. \(\pm i\tan\dfrac{\pi}{16},\ \pm i\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{16},\ \pm i\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{16},\ \pm i\tan\dfrac{7\pi}{16}\)
questions.hint: Let \(w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) so \(w^{8}=-1\): the 8th roots of \(-1\) lie on the unit circle at angles \(\theta=\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{8}\). Solve \(w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) for \(z\): \(z=\dfrac{1+w}{1-w}\) — exactly part (i)! Then \(z=i\cot\dfrac\theta2\).

steps.explain: Take the 8th root: \(w=e^{i\theta}\) with \(\theta=\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{8}\). Principal arguments: \(k=-4,-3,\dots,3\) (8 roots), all on the UNIT circle.
Solve \(w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) for \(z\): \(w(z+1)=z-1\Rightarrow wz+w=z-1\Rightarrow1+w=z(1-w)\).
This is exactly part (i) (valid because \(|w|=1\)): \(z=i\cot\dfrac\theta2=i\cot\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{16}\).
The 8 values of \(k\) give angles \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{16},\pm\dfrac{3\pi}{16},\pm\dfrac{5\pi}{16},\pm\dfrac{7\pi}{16}\). Since \(\cot(-x)=-\cot x\), the solutions come in \(\pm\) pairs.

All solutions are purely imaginary: they lie on the \(y\)-axis (the perpendicular bisector of \(-1\) and \(1\), since \(|z-1|=|z+1|\) when \(|w|=1\)). Why not the others: B uses \(\tan\); C uses the wrong angles (8th roots of \(+1\), not \(-1\)) and gives only 4 values; D gives only 4 of the 8 roots.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(w^{8}=-1\); \(z=\dfrac{1+w}{1-w}=i\cot\dfrac\theta2\).
